Classify new cases from a fitted model

Source: R/predict.R
predict.mixture_model.Rd

Computes the posterior class probabilities of cases that were not in the estimation sample, holding every parameter of the fitted model fixed. This is the E-step of the fitted model applied to new rows: by Bayes' rule a case's posterior is its class-specific likelihood times its prior class probability, normalised over classes. Vermunt and Magidson (2025) show that for the standard emissions this is exactly a logistic (or, with class-specific variances, quadratic) scoring equation, and that missing items change only its constant; running the E-step gives the same numbers without assembling the equation, missing values included.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'mixture_model'
predict(object, newdata, type = c("modal", "posterior", "both"), ...)

Arguments

object

A fitted model from fit_mixture().

newdata

A data frame or matrix holding the indicators (and the predictors, for a model that has them) of the cases to classify.

type

What to return, as in class_assignments(): "modal" the most probable class, "posterior" the matrix of posterior probabilities, "both" a data frame of the two.

...

Unused.

Value

One row (or element) per row of newdata, in the format class_assignments() returns; NA for a case that cannot be scored.

Details

Matching the new data to the fit. Indicators are matched to the fitted model's columns by name, so newdata may hold them in any order and may carry other columns. A factor or character indicator is coded against the levels it had when the model was fitted, never against the levels in newdata, and a value the fitted model never saw is an error rather than a silent mis-coding. A binary indicator that was recoded to 0/1 at fit time is recoded the same way. The same holds for a factor or character predictor: a level the model was not fitted with is an error, where scoring it would silently treat the case as belonging to the reference level.

Missing values. A missing answer simply drops out of that case's likelihood (full-information scoring), whether or not the estimation sample had any. A case missing every indicator has no information to classify on and gets NA, the same rule that dropped such rows from the estimation.

Predictors and distal outcomes. For a model with predictors (one step or three steps), the prior class probabilities are the fitted multinomial regression evaluated at the new case's predictors, so newdata must carry those columns; a factor predictor is supplied as the factor itself. A case with a missing predictor gets NA. A distal outcome is never used: a new case is classified from its indicators only, which is what keeps the outcome out of the classification (Vermunt and Magidson, 2025, sec. 1.4). For a model fitted with a distal outcome in one step, predict() on the estimation data therefore differs from class_assignments(), which conditions on the outcome too. It differs for a three-step model with predictors as well: there class_assignments() reports the step-3 posterior, which conditions on the step-1 class assignment, while predict() conditions on the indicators themselves, since a new case has no step-1 assignment. On a one-step model the two agree exactly.

Not covered. Latent transition models (scoring a sequence of statuses needs a choice between filtered and smoothed probabilities), growth models fitted from long data (fit_lcga(), fit_gmm(), fit_rmlca()), multiple-group models, models with direct effects of covariates on items (predictors_items), and models combining predictors with a distal outcome in one structural model are refused with an error.

References

Vermunt, J. K., & Magidson, J. (2025). Linear logistic scoring equations for latent class and latent profile models: A simple method for classifying new cases. Structural Equation Modeling, 32(3), 541–549. doi:10.1080/10705511.2024.2375736

See also

class_assignments() for the cases in the estimation sample.

Examples

set.seed(1)
X   <- matrix(rbinom(600, 1, rep(c(0.2, 0.8), each = 300)), ncol = 6,
              dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("u", 1:6)))
fit <- fit_mixture(X[1:80, ], n_classes = 2, measurement = "binary")
new <- X[81:100, ]
new[1, 2] <- NA                       # a missing answer is fine
predict(fit, new)
#>  [1] 1 1 2 1 2 1 1 1 2 1 1 1 1 2 1 1 1 2 2 1
head(predict(fit, new, type = "both"))
#>   class probability   Class 1     Class 2
#> 1     1   0.8380779 0.8380779 0.161922142
#> 2     1   0.8842124 0.8842124 0.115787629
#> 3     2   0.8790902 0.1209098 0.879090208
#> 4     1   0.9919797 0.9919797 0.008020265
#> 5     2   0.7016227 0.2983773 0.701622681
#> 6     1   0.9104523 0.9104523 0.089547688
